analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices after patents expire, allows personal imports from Canada, and penalizes deals that delay cheap generics.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate with zero cosponsors on March 3, 2020; the Finance Committee never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have lowered prescription drug prices several ways at once: Medicare would have to negotiate prices for patented Part D drugs once their patents ran out, with Medicaid's lowest price as a fallback if talks fail. Individuals could legally fill prescriptions at approved Canadian pharmacies for up to a 90-day supply. The FTC would get new power to fine deals where brand-name drug makers pay generic competitors to stay off the market, and to punish serial delay petitions. It also redesigns Medicare's drug benefit to cap a beneficiary's yearly out-of-pocket drug costs at $3,100, cut standard coinsurance from 25% to 20%, and eliminate the 'donut hole' coverage gap by requiring manufacturers to give discounts at the pharmacy counter.
analysis.who_benefits: People on Medicare, who would face a $3,100 annual out-of-pocket cap, lower coinsurance, no coverage gap, discounts applied at the pharmacy, and price negotiation on drugs whose patents have expired. Anyone who buys prescription drugs would gain the option of importing a 90-day personal supply from certified Canadian pharmacies. Generic and biosimilar makers would gain from faster market entry once pay-for-delay deals and delay petitions are penalized.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries and other prescription drug buyers

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would negotiate prices directly with manufacturers for patented Part D drugs after the patent period, and if no deal is reached within three months, the drug would be priced using the Medicaid 'best price' methodology.

Individuals could import a 90-day personal supply of prescription drugs from Canadian pharmacies the Health Secretary certifies, excluding controlled substances, biologics, and drugs needing refrigeration.

Agreements where a generic or biosimilar maker receives anything of value and agrees to delay its product would be presumed anticompetitive, with civil penalties of up to three times the value received.
Brand-name makers' filings with the FTC and Justice Department would require CEO certification that they are complete, and lying on the certification would have consequences.
Sham FDA petitions — filings aimed mainly at delaying generic approval — would draw FTC enforcement and civil penalties, plus referral of repeat delay petitions to the FTC.

Starting in 2022, Medicare drug plans would have to cap annual out-of-pocket costs at $3,100, cut standard coinsurance from 25% to 20%, and eliminate the coverage gap, funded by a manufacturer discount program providing discounts at the point of sale.
Plans would have to offer real-time benefit tools so doctors can see a patient's actual costs and cheaper alternatives while prescribing.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose prices for Medicare would become negotiable, whose pay-for-delay settlements with generic makers could be voided and fined, and who would owe point-of-sale discounts of up to 14% off the negotiated price under the new discount program. Pharmacy benefit managers and drug plans would face new data and transparency duties.

drawbacks.text: The negotiation mandate only applies after a drug's patents expire, so the newest — often most expensive — drugs would be untouched; the price pressure comes mainly from the Medicaid best price fallback rather than true negotiation of still-patented drugs.

Importing drugs adds a safety risk the bill manages rather than eliminates: it relies on Secretary certification of Canadian pharmacies and testing, and it excludes biologics, refrigerated drugs, and controlled substances, narrowing what patients can actually import.

A fair objection from the other side: lower negotiated prices and stiffer antitrust enforcement shrink brand-name drug revenue, which the industry argues would leave less money for developing new medicines; the bill includes no offsetting incentives for research.
The bill relies heavily on enforcement by an FTC and FDA whose diligence would vary by administration; a certification regime and referral procedures only bite if agencies pursue them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it targets — seniors and other Americans paying high drug prices — the provisions all point the same way: negotiated prices, a hard out-of-pocket cap, discounts at the counter, legal Canadian imports, and faster generic competition. The costs are real but smaller and largely borne by manufacturers: some safety risk on imports, possible drag on future drug development, and administrative burden on plans. The design weakness is that negotiation skips the newest patented drugs, so the bill is a meaningful price-lowering step rather than a complete fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled it for consideration, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Martha McSally introduced the bill on March 3, 2020 and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill's substance — Medicare negotiation, Canadian importation, pay-for-delay bans, and a Part D redesign with a $3,100 out-of-pocket cap — is described in the CRS summary and the bill text.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: their Medicare prices stayed non-negotiable, pay-for-delay settlements remained legal, and the coverage gap and current coinsurance stayed in place. Medicare beneficiaries saw no price relief.

for.name: Sen. Martha McSally
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona; bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its full drug-pricing package in the Senate.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.role: Chair, Senate Finance Committee (the committee the bill was referred to)
against.what_they_did: The Finance Committee took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote — and it died at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug makers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: The industry campaigned broadly against government negotiation of Medicare drug prices during this period; no industry position on this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no partisan breakdown; the sponsor was a Republican in a Congress where drug pricing split both parties internally.

industries.note: The bill makes their Medicare prices negotiable after patents lapse with a Medicaid best price fallback, bans and fines pay-for-delay settlements, penalizes sham delay petitions, and requires discounts of up to 14% off the negotiated price at the pharmacy counter. Their revenue from high U.S. prices is the direct target.
Pay-for-delay deals become presumed anticompetitive and sham petitions draw penalties, so generics and biosimilars reach the market sooner and these companies sell more volume sooner.
Secretary-certified Canadian pharmacies would be published on an FDA list as the legal channel for Americans buying 90-day personal supplies, creating a new customer stream.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The benefit redesign cuts federal reinsurance payments to plans and shifts cost-sharing onto manufacturer discounts, roughly offsetting; plans also must implement real-time benefit tools and pass discounts through at the point of sale.
